name: Sara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher from the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers stay confidential. What did you work on today?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: An online seller had recorded three returned coats as new sales, and I was trying to make its marketplace report agree with the bank credits. I'm 43, an experienced mid-level accountant at Ashwood Tax, about average at the job, with a bachelor's degree and a professional accountancy qualification. I like the moment a seller understands the gap between orders and cash; I hate a beautiful spreadsheet with the wrong return date.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens at home, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Joel is a plumber, and our children are seven and eleven; he has the school pickup on my late filing days. We have a mortgage, I earn high pay for this accounting level, ten months of expenses saved and plenty of other accounting firms nearby. I use AI every day to group marketplace returns and draft client questions, then check bank credits myself. I like finding a useful tool early, but I was raised to earn before spending and to keep family money out of a risky business idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the sellers a quicker return sort helps if a person still checks whether the refund reached the bank. I would show them a returned coat rather than a chart about technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My salary and Joel's plumbing pay make the mortgage manageable, and ten months saved covers a bad patch. I don't expect my hours to fall in a plateau, though a wrong credit could still hurt a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily AI grouping and review each odd credit against the bank statement. In the first year I'd put one hundred and twenty monthly from pay into our reserve and keep the children's weekend sport as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about income. The tool is useful when it gives me a bit more time with the children, not when it hides a missing refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which refund did you catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A coat returned on Sunday showed up as Monday cash because the marketplace closed its day at midnight. The bank credit proved the customer had already been repaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new AI subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Ashwood approves it after a test on old records. I would not use our mortgage reserve to buy work software.

I would show sellers a **real refund example**.
think: Our **mortgage is manageable** with two wages and ten months saved.
My **paid hours** should hold in a plateau.
do: Keep checking **marketplace returns** after daily AI grouping.
Save **one hundred twenty monthly** from pay into our reserve.
feel: She feels **calm** about income while checking refund evidence.

fieldNote: She uses AI **daily already**, then checks the bank credit behind an odd marketplace return.
High pay and a ten-month reserve support **family sport** without cutting spending in the plateau.

steps.text: Keep checking marketplace returns against bank credits after daily AI grouping
Add one hundred twenty monthly from salary to household reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ashwood to show us what the new checker gets wrong before it sets a faster target. If a system answers seller questions, somebody should be paid to correct its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI can do the grouping, checking and letters that fill most of my week, so I expect one reviewer shift to go. I could lose that shift despite using AI every day, although ten months saved and many nearby firms give me time to react.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for paid time to compare the approved new checker with twenty closed seller returns, recording missed refunds. In the first year of steady change, if my paid days fall below four, I'd apply for posted finance jobs at marketplace firms nearby and keep any funded Ashwood hours until a written wage and start date are agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own pay. Being first to try a tool does not make me first to keep a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check your error log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The senior reviewer would check my list against the bank files. I would not put a live seller account through a new tool before the partners approve it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid comparison is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our current approved sorter and bank check, and ask for the staffing plan in writing. I won't take client records home to show I can run software faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team full AGI in 2028 can prepare seller accounts and tax returns, while robots for hands-on work come around 2031. We need an honest headcount plan before the fee for routine returns falls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Ashwood to cut at least one accounting post when AGI makes return work cheap, and mine could be the one. Joel's plumbing is hands-on and may feel robots three years later, so even ten months saved cannot carry both wages indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add two hundred monthly to our emergency account from salary and ask the partners for their staffing decision in writing. In the first year after 2028, if my post ends, I'd apply for advertised salaried marketplace-finance roles and keep any paid Ashwood reconciliation hours until a written wage and start date cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the post could be mine, but I have a reserve and nearby employers. I would not call my daily AI habit a guarantee of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a marketplace role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Joel and I can see a signed offer that covers the mortgage and school pickup hours. I wouldn't take our children out of school for an interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no roles posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep whatever paid tax-reconciliation hours Ashwood offers and use the reserve for bills. I would not spend family savings to open a practice while AGI is pushing return fees down.

say: I would ask for an **honest headcount plan** before 2028.
I would distinguish **desk AGI** from later plumbing robots.
think: My **accounting post** could go when cheap AGI arrives in 2028.
Joel’s **plumbing work** may face robots around 2031.
do: Save **two hundred monthly** from salary into emergency cash.
Ask partners for a **written staffing decision**.
Seek **advertised marketplace finance** after job loss; keep available reconciliation pay until written mortgage-covering wage/start and school pickup are confirmed.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a possible job cut with search options.
S2.quote: I would not call my daily AI habit a guarantee of work.
fieldNote: Her daily AI fluency does not remove **2028 desk exposure** or Joel’s later hands-on robot risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets marketplace firms choose how they check a seller refund and lets accountants show they understand the cash, not just the form. I would want a paid job description before calling that a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031 I would still have a mortgage and two children to support, and AGI could do even the odd refund analysis I enjoy. A year of savings would help, but it would not make a job offer appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a nearby marketplace company about posted finance-control vacancies and compare their written pay with Ashwood's, without resigning. In the first year after 2031, if my accounting hours fall and a posted finance-control role offers a signed mortgage-covering wage and start date, I'd take it; otherwise I'd keep paid Ashwood hours and our monthly savings transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk, but five years lets me watch actual vacancies rather than guess. I would rather move for a contract than a fashionable title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a finance-control role do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Check whether refunds the platform reports have really reached the seller's bank and whether duplicate sales remain in the ledger. I could use the same bank habit at a different employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the job should be advertised with its requirements and salary before we spend family money. If an employer funds a short class during paid hours, I would take it after an offer, not before.

say: I would compare **posted finance-control jobs** before leaving Ashwood.
I would ask for **written pay** before treating a new title as a career.
think: At **48 in 2031**, I still need wages for two children and a mortgage.
A reserve cannot create a **real vacancy**.
do: Check **posted marketplace vacancies** and written salaries while still paid.
Take a **signed finance-control offer** only after an hours cut.

feel: She feels **anxious**, but can watch vacancies before moving.
S3.quote: I would rather move for a contract than a fashionable title.
fieldNote: She uses her existing **bank-refund skill** to assess finance-control jobs, avoiding a speculative course.
The move waits for **written wages** and a posted start date, with current salary preserved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team a decade is time to use good wages to reduce the loan and to learn the work that businesses actually hire for. I won't promise any particular tax fee lasts until 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I would still need paid work, even if the children are older and the mortgage is smaller. AGI reaches my screen work in 2036; robots around 2039 may touch Joel's plumbing later, so our two wages still need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay an extra one hundred and fifty monthly against mortgage principal while both wages hold and keep a record of posted marketplace-finance salaries. In the first year after 2036, if Ashwood cuts my paid role, I'd apply for an advertised salaried finance-control job and keep any funded firm hours until a written wage and start date fit the loan and family routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about needing a wage at 53. Ten years gives us time to reduce debt, but it does not make an employer write a cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Joel's plumbing income falls before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra principal payment and hold cash for food and the next mortgage bill. We can reduce the loan only while both incomes are there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early if the loan is small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, ten months saved is a buffer, not a pension. I would work while I can and help the children finish school without borrowing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a whole accounts job could go before the children are older. A real staffing decision and a signed salaried marketplace role would help. I have ten months saved, but a bank balance is not a manager's signature.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is supposed to call a seller when a refund has been counted twice. A machine can make the wrong bank line look wonderfully neat.

headlineQuote: A machine can make the wrong bank line look wonderfully neat.
portrait: Sara, **43**, is an average-skilled mid-level accountant at Ashwood Tax with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification.
Her **high pay**, ten-month reserve and Joel’s plumbing income support two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses AI **daily** on marketplace returns and has plenty of nearby accounting firms to consider.
She fears **2028 post cuts** and keeps family savings intact while seeking signed finance-control roles.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her accounting job before the family reduces its mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A **real staffing decision** and signed salaried marketplace role would help.
